h: The story behind the spectacle: broken voter rolls from Ballimaran to Lucknow
dek: Kalpana Sharma writes that in the noise over photographs of leaders climbing barricades, the ground evidence of how deep the trouble in the voter rolls runs is getting buried.
body: In her column on the media, Kalpana Sharma holds that the quarrel over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter rolls is not going to cool down. But the part television and newspapers keep their cameras fixed on is Rahul Gandhi climbing a barricade, Priyanka Gandhi lying on the road with the Constitution, and the social media display of young workers of the Cockroach Janata Party. According to the writer, all of this is spectacle; the news is somewhere else.

The first example is from Delhi. A Reporters' Collective investigation shows that the Commission's order to visit the homes of left-out voters means every booth officer has to reach an average of 215 homes in two months, while booth officers have their own jobs and many of them teach in schools. At 661 booths, 30 to 70 per cent of voters were stamped 'suspect'. In Ballimaran in old Delhi, 609 of the 635 names on the roll fell under that stamp.

In Bengal, the tribunals set up on the Supreme Court's orders cannot work at all, because even months later there is still no arrangement for sending notices from the Commission's portal. Uttar Pradesh's arithmetic is even more tangled: 71.38 lakh applications came on Form 6, but 84.3 lakh names were added to the final roll, which means 12.92 lakh names have no application on record at all.

The news from the Rejinagar and Nandigram bye-elections belongs to the same chain. The allegation is that in Muslim-majority Rejinagar many Muslims were sent back from booths, and local journalists' social media pages were kept shut until voting ended, so that no ground record would survive.

Sharma says that if these reports are read together the picture is clear: names cut, a stuck portal, names added with no paperwork, and the police's conduct in the bye-election. At the end of the column she points to the drought in Maharashtra, where 265 of 358 talukas are drought-hit, the country the camera does not easily reach.
nazar: This column is not a criticism of the movement but its memory. Anger on the street will last only if every rally carries with it the numbers from booths like Ballimaran. The poor, Muslim and migrant labourer families in the neighbourhoods where most names fell under suspicion in one sweep cannot rely on any camera; only on evidence can they get their vote back.
The lesson for the media is clear too: a photograph of a barricade sells for a day, an audit of the roll saves a democracy.
sawal: If 609 of 635 voters are suspect, who should the doubt fall on?
ref: Reporters' Collective
An independent group of investigative journalists that has published several investigations into SIR and voter roll data.
Booth Level Officer (BLO)
The official posted at every polling station, often a government schoolteacher, who goes door to door to check the voter roll.
ank: Names added to the UP roll with no application

h: The opposition is united; now the Election Commission has to answer
dek: In Deshbandhu, Rajesh Pandey argues that questions over the voter roll have given a scattered opposition a shared issue, but without ground-level organisation beyond rallies the job stays half done.
body: Rajesh Pandey sets two things side by side in this piece: the growing unity of the opposition, and the danger to democracy created by allegations of electoral mismanagement. In his view, the joint rally at Ramlila Maidan on 1 November, the cases filed in court and the activity of students and activists show that people's unease over the Election Commission's credibility is no longer limited to parties. Gyanesh Kumar stays silent and the BJP is on the defensive, but no answer to the flaws has come.

According to the writer, more than 13 crore names were removed from the rolls through SIR, and once the flaws came to light the Commission had to withdraw the changes to Form 6 and set up an expert committee to review ECINET. Two election commissioners recorded written objections that some big decisions were taken in the Commission's name without their knowledge, while the Commission tells the Supreme Court that the decisions were unanimous.

The mismatch in UP's voter data, the suspension of two electoral registration officers in Pilibhit, the cutting of 99.32 lakh names in Karnataka and nearly 61,000 Form 7s filled without reason: in the writer's eyes these are the kind of failures for which no one has yet been held to account. On Amit Shah's claim of three crore infiltrators, he asks why, if it is true, they have not been sent out of the country.

The piece recalls the Lohia years, the Janata Party of 1977 and the Janata Dal of 1989, most of which lasted only a short while. According to the writer, the difference this time is that the issue is the honesty of elections and the accountability of the Commission, which can become common ground that brings everyone together.

But the conclusion carries a warning too: rallies alone will not be enough. The Congress in particular, which the writer sees as weak in organisation, will have to send its workers into villages and neighbourhoods. He is confident that when public pressure holds, institutions answer.
nazar: The strength of the piece is its list: from Form 6 to Form 7 and on to Pilibhit, it shows that the charges are not in the air but rest on solid administrative lapses, though figures like 13 crore are the writer's own and should be independently checked. The weakness is that Rahul Gandhi's leadership is praised with a little too much confidence, while the tug of war over seats in the states is still to come.

The most useful point is in the last paragraph. Jantar Mantar and Ramlila Maidan built the mood, but the person whose name has been cut stands alone at the booth. The movement's next test will be there.
sawal: Who will fight the battle over cut names at the booth level?
ref: Form 7

An application to object to a name on the voter roll or to get it removed.
Under the rules, reasons have to be given in it.
ECINET

The Election Commission's integrated digital platform.
Voter registration and roll-related work runs on it.

h: Fourteen objections from two commissioners: why a resignation is needed
dek: According to P. John J. Kennedy, the evidence against Gyanesh Kumar came not from outside but from inside the Commission, and the real root is the 2023 appointment law.
body: Kennedy separates two questions: can any group force a resignation by pressure, and is there solid ground behind this demand. The answer to the first has already come in Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation. For the second, the writer looks at the Commission's own papers.

Citing an Indian Express investigation, he says election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded written objections at least fourteen times in ten months, four times in a single day. The rule says decisions are to be taken by consensus or by majority. The writer's argument is that when two of three members disagree in writing and the decision is still carried out, the process has broken down.

He counts three examples. Joshi's objection to centralising ECINet, the digital system for voter data, because it cuts the power of district officers who hold the legal authority to add or remove names. The 97 voters of Goa, whom the local officer found eligible, but the software would not let the decision be recorded. And the question in Form 6 of parents or grandparents being on the old roll, for which no change was made in the rules. Who is responsible for the nearly 16 lakh appeals filed in Bengal in the Commission's name is something the two commissioners could not settle either.

According to the writer, the root is the 2023 law, which removed the Chief Justice from the selection committee and seated a minister of the Prime Minister's choosing instead, so that the government has two votes out of three. Without that change, changing the face will achieve nothing.

Even so, he argues for a voluntary resignation. The constitutional process for removal is very hard, and a forced exit will look like a defeat, while a resignation would send the message that the office understands its responsibility. The other lapses need a separate audit.
nazar: This piece gives the movement a necessary discipline: the slogan may be against one man, but the demand should be about the whole structure. The call to roll back the appointment law, in resolutions passed from Ramlila Maidan to Bengaluru, comes from this understanding. The story of Goa's 97 voters shows that when software grows bigger than the officer, the first to lose is the one with no route to complain.
sawal: If two of three commissioners disagree in writing, whose decision should stand?
ref: ECINet
The Election Commission's integrated digital platform, which handles data for the voter roll and election work.
Chief Election Commissioner Act 2023
The appointment law in which the selection committee has the Prime Minister, a union minister and the Leader of the Opposition; the Chief Justice was left out.

h: The 'infiltrator': failed every time, yet the same tune
dek: In Deshbandhu, the editor of Lok Lehar argues that SIR cut crores of names but found only thousands of foreigners, and that even after Ramlila Maidan the BJP has no answer except the fear of the 'infiltrator'.
body: The writer sees the 1 November rally as the beginning of the end of 'Modi-shahi' (Modi's rule), because in his eyes the Sangh and the BJP have gone back to the same old tool to answer the campaign over stolen votes: the fear that infiltrators have not merely entered the country but have spread across it. Amit Shah said the complaints about names being cut in SIR were really an attempt to protect infiltrators.

According to the piece, for more than twelve years the Home Ministry has been saying in answers to Parliament and to RTI requests that it has no solid figure for infiltrators. Assam's NRC is the example: after heavy expense and hardship for the poor, about 20 lakh people came under the shadow of doubtful citizenship, and when it turned out that two-thirds of them were Hindu, the writer says the BJP government itself rejected the NRC.

The writer says SIR repeated the same story. In Bihar about one crore names were cut, but the Commission did not say how many of them were foreigners; according to the piece, fewer than 600 foreigners turned up among more than six crore voters. Citing media investigations, he says that checks of 9.96 crore voters in six states found only 1,600 foreigners, and among the 99.7 lakh names cut in Karnataka 716 were foreigners, 545 of them Nepali.

The most interesting fact is from Uttar Pradesh. According to the piece, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said at a party meeting that 1.27 crore Hindu votes had been cut in the state, and asked workers to reconnect them through the BJP's 'Kamal app'. For the writer this exposes the declared purpose of SIR.

The conclusion is that infiltrators mostly live in propaganda, while the real price is paid by poor and marginalised Hindus, Muslims and women, whose vote and citizenship are both at stake. The BJP president's claim of 'three crore infiltrators', according to the writer, is the return of the same failed weapon.
nazar: The most effective part of the piece is its count: crores of names cut, foreigners a thousand or two. If these figures are right, and the writer is bringing them from media investigations, then the declared purpose of SIR and its result do not match. This question should be put to the Commission, not to the BJP.

A prediction like 'the beginning of the end' is written in heat; read it that way. But the lesson of the NRC matters: the fear of the 'infiltrator' falls first on the poor who are weak on papers, whatever their religion.
sawal: Among crores of cut names, why only a few thousand foreigners?
ref: Kamal app

The BJP's own app.
According to the piece, it was suggested for re-adding cut names in UP.
Lok Lehar
A Hindi weekly linked to the CPI(M).
photo_note: Representative image: students protesting against CAA-NRC

h: Rishi Anand: this is not a lapse, it is a conspiracy against the republic
dek: On his Substack, Rishi Anand alleges that the Chief Election Commissioner misled both the court and the public, and that the accounting for this should go beyond impeachment.
body: Rishi Anand's piece is in no mood for softness. He starts with the Indian Express report that detailed fourteen written disagreements by two election commissioners: being kept in the dark about decisions, agendas and minutes of meetings not being prepared, changes made in forms without approval, and the centralisation of voter data. According to the writer, the Commission's defensive press release confirmed these things rather than denying them.

In his eyes the matter is bigger than this. In June 2025, a few months before the Bihar election, SIR was announced suddenly, but there is no record of any meeting or assessment, and applications under the Right to Information were sent back too. Across the country 13.37 crore names were cut from the draft rolls. The writer estimates that one adult in seven may be off the roll, and that by placing the burden of proof on the citizen the vote has been turned from a right into a favour.

About Bengal he claims that an unaudited software flagged 1.3 crore voters for 'logical discrepancy', 27 lakh names were cut, and after the election 91 per cent of the appeals in the tribunals went in the voter's favour, but by then the chance to vote had gone. 'Infiltrators' were talked about again and again, but their count was never made public.

The list of charges also includes giving scanned copies in place of machine-readable rolls, cases filed in Bihar against journalists who showed the truth, and demanding an affidavit from Rahul Gandhi while staying silent on a similar claim by Anurag Thakur.

In conclusion Anand demands a sedition case against Gyanesh Kumar, his arrest, and the scrapping of the 2023 appointment law, which also gave election commissioners immunity from legal action over official decisions.
nazar: This piece is a sample of the movement's sharpest voice, and several of its claims are still charges, not a court's finding. Even so, its central question is fair: why does an institution that asked crores of people to prove they exist shrink from giving a record of its own decisions? In Bengal, 91 per cent of appeals going in the voter's favour shows who carried the cost of the error: the poor and minority voter, who lost the vote and then queued up for justice.
sawal: Who will draw the line between carelessness and conspiracy?
ref: Logical discrepancy
A flag raised by software in SIR, such as a mismatch in name or age, after which a notice is sent to the voter.

h: Siyasat: the questions are for the Commission, so why is the BJP answering?
dek: The editorial in Siyasat, Hyderabad's Urdu daily, says vote theft is now the people's issue, and that Amit Shah entering the field has not lessened the doubt but deepened it.
body: This Siyasat editorial, published on the day of the Ramlila Maidan rally, holds that the question of vote theft is no longer the opposition parties' alone. Students, activists, lawyers and civil society are raising it and public opinion is taking shape. According to the paper, an English daily exposed the allegedly arbitrary and one-sided decisions of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, and since then the issue has been at the centre of the national debate.

The editorial's complaint is that the Commission has offered no explanation so far. Talk of differences among the three commissioners came into the open, but they neither appeared together nor answered the charges. Instead BJP leaders, union ministers and chief ministers came out to answer, and now Amit Shah too has spoken of running campaigns against the opposition in several states and of a debate or a special session in Parliament.

The paper's argument is simple: the opposition, the young and students are not asking the government, they are asking the Election Commission. In such a situation the BJP answering on the Commission's behalf is beyond its brief and out of place. According to the editorial, every defence the BJP puts up deepens the doubt and raises new questions, because the charge is that it was the one that gained from the Commission's wrong decisions.

The paper mentions Maharashtra, where, it says, about 40 lakh votes were added in the eight months before the assembly election, and Bengal and Bihar, where lakhs of names were cut and are being restored after the election. The editorial's demand is that the government stay out; the Commission should answer for itself.

The second part of the piece is on price rise. Everyday things are moving out of the reach of ordinary families, and the paper demands action against hoarding. Its warning is that economic hardship is stoking people's anger further.
nazar: Siyasat has caught a small but important point: when the ruling party starts answering questions raised about a constitutional institution, it itself becomes a witness against that institution's independence. The pairing of the Commission's silence and the home minister's loudness is the movement's biggest argument.
Bringing price rise into it is not beside the point either. The right to vote and the right to bread are not separate fights, and for readers of an Urdu paper both are part of daily life.
sawal: Why should the home minister answer for the Commission's silence?
ref: Siyasat

An Urdu daily published from Hyderabad since 1949.
It has deep reach among Muslim readers in south India.
photo_note: Representative image: a pile of newspapers

h: Ravish Kumar: in the noise about 'regime change', Gyanesh Kumar gets a shield
dek: Writing in The Wire Urdu, Ravish Kumar says that instead of answering questions about vote theft the government threw the charge of 'regime change' at the opposition, so that eyes would not rest on the Chief Election Commissioner.
body: Ravish Kumar says the real 'regime change' is the one in which people are robbed of their right to vote and so left without the very tool for changing power. In his view the government gave no answer to SIR and the charges of vote theft; instead it turned the debate around by accusing the opposition of plotting to topple the government.

The writer recalls that the government stayed quiet at first, then SIR was tied to infiltration. Amit Shah said Rahul Gandhi was protesting to protect infiltrators. Ravish asks why the number of infiltrators found in this exercise, running since June last year, has still not come out, when the Supreme Court had given the Home Ministry the job of investigating such cases.

Citing Assam's NRC, he says more than 1,500 crore rupees were spent there, many Hindus were also pushed out, and once the work was done the BJP abandoned it. According to the writer, the same story has now come back through SIR. If the opposition had not got the basis accepted as valid documents in court, he claims, a very large number of people would have fallen off the roll.

He also questions the dismissal of Gen Z's quiet protests at Jantar Mantar as 'mental Naxalism'. He calls the names cut in Bihar and Bengal illegal and an irreversible loss, and asks why the Commission was not awake when forms were being filled in bulk.

The piece concludes that the 'regime change' row is a curtain to save Gyanesh Kumar. The Commission itself does not face the press's questions, and the ban at Jantar Mantar will not bring back its credibility. The sense of Ravish's words is that vote theft is an attack on the soul of democracy, and calling it a ghost is meant to turn people's attention away.
nazar: This piece is three weeks old, but today it seems even truer: even after Ramlila Maidan the government's answer is coming not from the Commission but from the home minister and BJP leaders. Ravish's sharpest question is the one still unanswered: where is the count of infiltrators?

The comparison with the NRC gives this debate a history. Assam showed that the 'infiltrator' stamp comes first and the proof never arrives, and in between the poorest and those weakest on papers keep running after it.
sawal: Which question is the noise about 'regime change' burying?
ref: NRC

The National Register of Citizens.
In Assam, more than 19 lakh people were left out of its final list in 2019.
Regime change

The charge of a plot to topple the government.
The BJP has levelled exactly this charge at the opposition's movement.

h: Local body elections in Pakistan: every government's favourite excuse
dek: Dawn's editorial says provincial governments change the law itself to put off local body elections, and the ordinary citizen pays.
body: Pakistan's big parties swear by the Constitution, but they shy away from giving people the right to elect a government for their street and neighbourhood. According to Dawn's editorial, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, after the emergency, Article 140-A of the Constitution was suspended first in some districts and then across the province, and because of this the Election Commission simply dropped preparations for local body elections there. The term of the previous bodies there ended in June.

The elections due in Islamabad on 20 December are also up in the air, because the delimitation has been challenged in the High Court. Punjab is to vote in February 2027, provided no new hurdle is raised. The law says elections must be held within 120 days of a term ending, but Punjab's election has been pending since May 2022 and Islamabad's since June 2021.

The editorial points to a familiar trick: whichever party is in power in the province changes the local government law, so that delimitation is done afresh and the election slides further. This wastes public money and leaves people without their closest representatives.

The paper suggests two routes. First, amend the Elections Act 2017 so that a body's law cannot be changed after its term ends. Second, write the local election process clearly into the Constitution itself, so that neither the centre nor the province can escape.

The editorial also reminds that strong and accountable local bodies are needed for the development of cities, towns and villages. A democratic alternative to the disputed debate over new provinces is exactly this: that power and money reach down.
nazar: This debate is not only Pakistan's. In India too, municipal and panchayat elections in several states have been put off for years and administrators have been left to run things. Where power shrinks upward, the lowest and closest step of democracy breaks first. Dawn's suggestion, that the door to changing the rules be shut, is worth thinking about in both countries.
sawal: Without local government, whose door does democracy reach?
ref: Article 140-A
The provision of Pakistan's Constitution that obliges every province to set up local government and hand it political, administrative and financial authority.

h: Nepal: fast decisions are no substitute for accountability
dek: In The Kathmandu Post a young writer asks why Balen Shah's government avoids Parliament's questions, and where a mind made up by reels will take democracy.
body: Nepal's politics is fast and dramatic these days, and young people are watching it more closely than before, but mostly through reels, TikTok and short posts. Ashswi Karki, a law student, says this same weakness in information is serving the government's purpose. He counts four kinds of supporters: those who accept every claim without checking, those who believe being young is itself a guarantee of being better, people satisfied with quick relief, and the blind followers of Prime Minister Balendra Shah. According to the writer, together these can build the road to a long 'democratic dictatorship'.

The state of Parliament is the solid reason for his worry. Rule 56 of the House rules says MPs must get time in the first week of every month to question the Prime Minister. But there is no penalty for not turning up. According to the writer, by the end of July Shah had come before the House only once, and even after the Speaker's direction in August he was mostly absent until the session ended in October, and the Speaker himself is from the ruling party.

There is a question over ordinances too. Article 114 of the Constitution allows an ordinance only when Parliament is not in session and there is an urgent need. The writer alleges that the government called Parliament, prorogued the session before it could sit, and then issued ordinances. About 1,600 political appointments were removed, but key posts were left vacant.

Citing an investigation by Kantipur, he says that by the end of a hundred days only 38 of the government's hundred promises had been kept. According to the writer, with showy steps the root problems of corruption and the flight of talent stay exactly where they were.
The writer's remedy is simple: the Prime Minister should answer in the House, ordinances should come only in a real emergency, and citizens should test every claim before passing it on.
nazar: After the Gen Z movement in Nepal people had great hopes from the government that came in. This piece matters because the criticism comes from within the same generation that demanded change. A new face does not make institutions unnecessary; answering questions in Parliament is as necessary for any popular leader as it was for old leaders. In South Asia the mix of charismatic leaders and social media has pushed accountability aside again and again, so this warning should be heard on this side of the border too.
sawal: Should a popular leader be exempt from Parliament's questions?
ref: Article 114
The provision of Nepal's Constitution that lets the government issue an ordinance only when Parliament is not in session and there is an urgent need.
Rule 56
The rule in the rules of Nepal's House of Representatives under which time is fixed in the first week of every month to question the Prime Minister directly.

h: In Turkey, when does a joke become a crime?
dek: In Jacobin, Dora Mengüç writes that the case against comedian Deniz Göktaş shows that in Erdoğan's Turkey the limits of laughter are now set by courts and prisons.
body: Stand-up comedian Deniz Göktaş, 32, performed his hour-and-a-half show 'Ölü Deniz' (Dead Sea) 198 times in three years before more than a lakh people, and not one complaint came. The trouble began when he did it on a big stage in Istanbul and put it on YouTube. Edited clips spread and 185 complaints reached the government's complaint portal, most of which, Göktaş says, had not seen the full show.

On 2 July he was taken into custody at Istanbul airport. The charges were insulting President Erdoğan, inciting hatred and praising a crime. He spent 88 days in a high-security prison, with no sunlight and no talking to other inmates. On 28 September the court acquitted him of praising a crime, but sentenced him to 11 months and 20 days for insulting the President and seven and a half months for insulting religious values, then released him.

Göktaş's argument was that calling Erdoğan a 'dictator' is a political assessment, not abuse, and that the powerful should be able to take a joke. His friend and fellow comedian Emre Günsal, who himself had to go to prison in 2020 over a clip, says the real damage is fear: when no one knows where the line is, artists cut their own material before they even write it. According to law professor Tolga Şirin, the crime of incitement is made out only when there is a clear and immediate danger to public safety, not by the count of complaints.

The writer links this to the tradition that runs from the satirical paper Markopaşa of Aziz Nesin and Sabahattin Ali to the Gezi Park movement, which every era's rulers have laid hands on. One line of Göktaş's tells the whole story: in America there is cancel culture; here we have cancel culture too, and prison as well.
nazar: Indian readers will not find this story strange. Here too comedians' shows have been cancelled, FIRs have been filed against them, and crowds have broken up stages. The most dangerous part is what Günsal says: when the limit is left blurred, the artist puts a lock on his own tongue. Satire is a mirror to power, and a regime that fears the mirror is really afraid of its own face.
sawal: What is a power that guards laughter afraid of?
ref: CİMER
The Turkish government's online portal for complaints and applications, through which 185 complaints were filed against Göktaş's show.
photo_note: A rich man, Gaganendranath Tagore's caricature

h: Riyadh's blasphemy law, Gujarat's cow slaughter law: the same logic
dek: In Scroll, Shoaib Daniyal argues that India, which gives life imprisonment for 'insult' to a religious symbol, is walking the very path it condemns Saudi Arabia for.
body: Last month a court in Saudi Arabia sentenced 27-year-old Sri Lankan Anojan Shivarasa to death for allegedly insulting Islam and the Prophet. There was an outcry across the world, the sentence was reversed, but he was not acquitted and is still in prison. Against this, Shoaib Daniyal sets the Indian ruling of 28 October, in which a Gujarat court gave three Muslims rigorous life imprisonment for the crime of cow slaughter.

According to the writer, the judge leaned on the Vedas and the Manusmriti in the judgment, called the cow the pivot of faith, and mentioned that 33 crore gods reside in it. In Gujarat the penalty for cow slaughter can be as heavy as for murder. The Deputy Chief Minister praised the verdict and supporters celebrated it as if it were a declaration of a 'Hindu rashtra'.

After the First World War Gandhi brought cow protection into national politics, but he favoured persuasion, not punishment. Within two years of his assassination a ban on cow slaughter entered the Directive Principles of the Constitution, which cannot be enforced through the courts. States then made their own laws, and in 2005, with Modi as Chief Minister, Gujarat made a harsher law, which the Supreme Court also upheld.

The writer alleges that after Modi became Prime Minister, mobs repeatedly took the lives of Muslims in the name of cow protection, and these gangs got official protection. He gives the example of Monu Manesar, accused in 2023 of burning two Muslims alive, who is not in jail.

Daniyal accepts that India is not a monarchy like Saudi Arabia; in 1949 the Constituent Assembly chose the path of making laws on secular reasoning. But his worry is that powerful forces want to reverse that decision. Those who rightly criticise Riyadh's blasphemy law forget that at home they are backing laws of the same kind.
nazar: This comparison is uncomfortable, but necessary. Protecting one religion's sacred symbol with the power of the state, and punishing other citizens in its name, is the real mark of blasphemy laws, whether the symbol is a book or an animal. When a court writes a judgment citing scripture and the government celebrates it, the Constitution's secularism stays in the book, not on the ground. The first to pay for it are Muslims, Dalits and the poor in the animal trade.
sawal: Why does the Constitution's secular promise stall at the courtroom door?
ref: Directive Principles
The principles in Part Four of the Constitution, which guide the government but cannot be enforced through the courts; Article 48 speaks of banning cow slaughter.
photo_note: Cleansing in muddy water, Gaganendranath Tagore's caricature

h: Trump lost, but who will stop America's wars?
dek: In Middle East Eye, Sami al-Arian writes that the Democratic sweep in the midterms is a verdict against the Iran war, but a majority in Congress does not mean an anti-war majority.
body: In the 3 November midterms the Democrats won both houses. According to Sami al-Arian, director of the Centre for Islam and Global Affairs at Istanbul Zaim University, they have at least 54 seats in the Senate, seven taken from the Republicans, Kansas elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 1932 and Texas for the first time since 1988.

The writer sees the root of this defeat in the attack on Iran. In the exit polls he cites, 63 per cent of voters called the attack wrong, 87 per cent were worried about fuel prices and only 38 per cent were happy with Trump's work. Because of the disruption in Hormuz, petrol reached about 4.27 dollars a gallon by the end of October. Vice President Vance put the blame for the defeat squarely on the war. He sees the victories of Abdul al-Sayed, who spoke openly about Gaza in Michigan, and of James Talarico, who refused AIPAC's money in Texas, as proof of this shift.

But al-Arian warns against wishful thinking. It was the Biden administration that gave Israel weapons in the Gaza war and vetoed a ceasefire resolution at the United Nations. Citing Brown University's Costs of War, he says that in the two years after 7 October 2023 America gave Israel at least 21.7 billion dollars in military aid. At least 11 newly elected members are supporters of Palestinian rights, yet the party leadership still treats Israel as a central ally.

From January the new Congress can put a brake on the war and on arms sales through investigations, subpoenas and conditions on the budget, but it does not have the two-thirds majority needed to override a veto. There is also the fear that the outgoing Congress may lock in a heavy military budget for Israel first. His conclusion is that an election change is not a structural change; the structure that keeps wars going is still standing.
nazar: The American voter has said plainly that he does not want to pay for distant wars out of his own pocket. But history shows that in Washington the policy of war has been shared property of both parties. The real test will be whether the new Congress only corners Trump or also breaks that consensus which brought devastation to Gaza and Iran. For the Global South this question is not merely America's internal affair, because the blow of Hormuz closing fell on oil and fertiliser prices from Delhi to Dhaka.
sawal: Can voters' anger change the direction of the war machine?
ref: AIPAC
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a powerful pro-Israel lobby that spends heavily for and against candidates in US elections.
Lame-duck session
The sittings of the old Congress after an election and before the new one is sworn in, in which defeated members also vote.
photo_note: A snowstorm: Hannibal's army crossing the Alps

h: Netanyahu's slide and Modi's Israeli bet
dek: In The Federal, D. Ravi Kanth asks where India's diplomacy and its morality will stand once the leader Modi grew so close to leaves power.
body: In Israel's election last month no party won a majority of 60 seats. On 7 November President Isaac Herzog invited Gadi Eisenkot to form a government, whose broad coalition has outside support from the Arab-Palestinian parties with 19 seats. Eisenkot rejected Netanyahu's offer of a 'unity government' and said his aim was to remove the leader responsible for the failure of 7 October 2023. Netanyahu said Qatar had a hand in the Arab parties' victory.

D. Ravi Kanth recalls that Netanyahu, hemmed in by International Criminal Court arrest warrants and corruption trials, has been among Modi's closest foreign friends. He had invited Modi to Israel's 2027 independence day celebrations, and on 28 February, two days before the attack on Iran, the Israeli parliament honoured Modi. The writer calls that war illegal and asks whether the invitation still stands.

Netanyahu's troubles are outside home too. According to the writer, Trump announced that by the end of this year, two years before the current agreement ends, about 4 billion dollars a year in military aid to Israel will stop, and Herzog said he had had no inkling of it. In September, when Netanyahu spoke at the UN General Assembly, most countries got up and walked out.

The writer's criticism of India is sharp. Modi at once called the killing of seven Israelis in Tel Aviv 'heinous', but stayed silent on the deaths of Palestinian civilians and the devastation in Gaza. The RSS invited the Israeli ambassador to its hundredth foundation ceremony. India is a signatory to the 1948 Genocide Convention, while the International Court of Justice is hearing genocide charges against Israel; in the writer's view, a new bilateral investment treaty with Israel can be seen as complicity under international law.
nazar: The risk of resting foreign policy on one leader's personal friendship is this: the leader goes, but the stain of having stood with him stays. For decades India raised its voice for Palestine's rights and that credibility was its capital in the Global South. Silence on Gaza and closeness during the war have shrunk that capital. If power is changing in Israel itself, this is the chance for Delhi to return to its old, principled line.
sawal: In a diplomacy of friendship, where is room left for principles?
ref: Genocide Convention (1948)
The United Nations treaty that makes genocide an international crime and obliges signatory countries to prevent it and not to be complicit in it.

h: Showing violence at a procession is not hatred: FIR against journalist quashed
dek: The Madhya Pradesh High Court has quashed the case against Uvesh Khan, a YouTube journalist from Raisen, saying that reporting a clash is not in itself a crime.
body: In Silwani town of Raisen district, on 6 September last year, there were scuffles at two places during the Ganesh immersion. Around nine at night a man was hit on the head with a lathi, and there was a second clash near the nearby Shiva temple. Uvesh Khan, a freelance journalist who runs a channel called 'Uvesh Reporter', posted a video of it. A big TV channel also showed the incident, and its report said the CCTV footage showed police standing and watching.

The next day Khan got calls to take the video down and he did. Even so, on 8 September an FIR was filed against him under Section 196(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, on a complaint by a man named Rajeev Soni. The complaint said the video's title, which spoke of a 'bloody clash' and two people seriously injured, spread fear and confusion among the Hindu community.

In his order of 28 October, Justice Himanshu Joshi quashed the case. Citing earlier Supreme Court rulings, the court said the offence under this section is made out only when there is an intent to stir enmity between at least two communities. Hurt feelings in one community alone are not enough. The FIR had not named even one word that would stir enmity.

The court also held that reporting a sensitive incident cannot by itself put a stop to freedom of speech, and that carrying the case on would be a misuse of the legal process. According to Alt News, Khan's reach fell after the FIR, and a source says the same news ran in many other places that day, but the crosshairs were on him alone.
nazar: YouTube journalists in small towns are often alone, with neither an institution behind them nor a team of lawyers. One complaint and one section can stop their work for months. The High Court's ruling is a relief, but the process had already become the punishment: a case running fourteen months and a shrinking livelihood. The question also stands of why, when a big channel showed the same incident, the case was filed only against Uvesh Khan.
sawal: One story, many channels, so why was the case only against Uvesh?
ref: Section 196 of the Sanhita

This section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaces Section 153A of the old IPC.
It makes spreading enmity between groups on grounds of religion, caste or language a crime.

h: Supreme Court on Delhi's air: restrictions alone will not get the job done
dek: At the pollution hearing the court asked for reports instead of issuing directions, and set aside a doctor's account of children's lungs as a story.
body: In the case it started on its own over pollution in Delhi-NCR, the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana indicated that the court's intervention should stay limited, because too many orders only encourage violations. The bench suggested that an understanding of pollution be built into Diwali celebrations themselves, with councillors and neighbourhood committees appealing to people not to burn things.

A chest surgeon at Ganga Ram Hospital said the lungs of Delhi's children are not healthy. The bench said it would go not by such personal opinion but by expert bodies and the GRAP recommendations, unless some peer-reviewed research says otherwise. A lawyer mentioned a 2012 study in which schoolchildren's lung capacity was found to be 43.5 per cent lower. Justice Bagchi also opposed closing schools, counting the weaknesses of online study.

Amicus curiae Aparajita Singh said the air is close to the 'severe' category and that by 5 November stubble's share in pollution was 14 per cent. She said running subsidised machines is expensive and of no use for small farms. The Chief Justice suggested giving the machines to panchayats and fixing the purchase rate in advance.

On vehicles at the border left with engines running, the additional solicitor general accepted that the earlier orders were not fully enforced. The Centre said diesel autos will be phased out by 1 January 2027. In the end the bench asked officials for reports instead of giving any directions.
nazar: The court saying that restrictions do not work is both honest and worrying. When the AQI is touching 400 and the amicus is explaining that the city's average hides the poison of street after street, then accepting 'bad' air as normal is the biggest defeat. The price is paid by the children who play outside and the workers who work on the road, who have neither an air purifier nor leave to stay at home.
sawal: How much smoke does the evidence of children's lungs need before it counts as proof?
ref: GRAP

The Graded Response Action Plan, a scheme of step-by-step restrictions according to the state of the air.
It is enforced by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM).

h: Mosques in Barmer and Jaisalmer: a hearing must come before the bulldozer
dek: The Jodhpur bench of the Rajasthan High Court said structures cannot be pulled down without hearing the reply to a notice and without a written, reasoned order.
body: The Jodhpur bench of the High Court gave an important order on 6 November on the bulldozer action against mosques and shrines in Rajasthan's border districts. Hearing five appeals, the bench of Justice Vineet Kumar Mathur and Justice Chandrashekhar Sharma said the people affected must get a full and fair chance to put their case.

The main case was Ghafoor vs the State of Rajasthan. The appellants' lawyers argued that the administration was pulling down structures without taking or considering replies to show-cause notices. The government assured the court that nothing would be demolished until a decision was taken on the notice proceedings. The court asked the appellants to reply in detail within two weeks, and the officer must then hold a hearing, look at all the documents and pass a written, reasoned order.

On the strength of that order the appeals relating to two mosques in Barmer and the Pokhran area of Jaisalmer were also disposed of. According to Jamiat Ulama-e-Rajasthan, the drive began on 18 June and fourteen mosques and shrines have already been pulled down. On 13 July the High Court dismissed more than forty petitions, after which the Supreme Court gave a fifteen-day interim stay and opened the way to appeal before a division bench.

The Jamiat alleges that a delegation of its was stopped from visiting the affected areas. A second team that went in October says villagers had built these mosques themselves in remote sandy areas. A large part of the news rests on the Jamiat's press release; the government's side is not in it.
nazar: The order says nothing new; it only repeats what is the foundation of the law: hear first, then decide. But when fourteen places of worship are already down, this reminder is a relief that came late. For the desert villages that built these mosques with their own hands, the real test is yet to come, when the officer actually hears them or only goes through the motions.
sawal: Who will hold the hearing for the fourteen places of worship already down?
ref: Show-cause notice

A notice sent to the affected party before any action.
It asks why the action should not be taken, and the reply has to be considered.

h: How were power and water cut without notice: High Court on Race Course mosque
dek: On the appeal of the Waqf-registered and heritage-listed mosque near the Prime Minister's residence, the Delhi High Court asked the NDMC and the Waqf Board to reply.
body: The Delhi High Court raised questions on Friday over the cutting of power and water to the Race Course mosque, which stands inside the Race Course Club in New Delhi. During the hearing Justice Subramonium Prasad said plainly that electricity cannot be cut without notice, especially when the building is a notified property.

The appeal was filed by the mosque's imam, Mohammed Haroon, against the order of a single judge on 15 October that refused to restore the facilities. The bench of Justice Prasad and Justice Renu Bhatnagar issued notice to the New Delhi Municipal Council and the Delhi Waqf Board and sought replies in two weeks. The next hearing is on 14 December.

The imam's lawyer, M. Sufiyan Siddiqui, said the officers had leaned on a decision in another matter, one connected to encroachment by three slum clusters opposite the Prime Minister's residence, in which the mosque side was not a party. After that order about seven hundred families were evicted in August. According to the appeal, the real question is whether the council has the right to stop the power and water of a working mosque and its hujra, and whether the single judge's order rests on a wrong reading of the Waqf law.

Since 2009 the mosque has been recorded as Waqf property and a Grade II heritage building. On this land of the roughly 53-acre club a campaign to get the land back to the Centre is on. On 29 October the Centre told the court that within four weeks a decision would be taken on the Waqf Board's application, and that until then there would be no coercion. Meanwhile the Centre has also told the court that it intends to remove the old mosque in the Krishi Bhavan complex.
nazar: Cutting a building's power and water before demolishing it is an old method: the bulldozer comes later, the ruin begins earlier. If this is happening to a heritage mosque standing in the area closest to power, think what must be happening in distant settlements. The court's question is right, but while the answer is awaited the mosque will stay dark until December.
sawal: How many days will heritage status save it from the lights going out?
ref: Hujra

A small room attached to a mosque, where the imam or the muezzin usually lives.
In this case the cutting of its power is what has been challenged.

h: Nokaip's Facebook page will return; government says it never ordered a block
dek: In the Kerala High Court the government admitted it had only asked for a few comments to be taken down, yet a Malayalam news page stayed blocked in India for five weeks.
body: The Facebook page of the Malayalam digital news platform Nokaip stopped being visible in India on 28 September. Meta said this was done on a notice from the central government or a law enforcement agency under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT law. Editor-in-chief Haider Ali K. knocked on the High Court's door. He said the blocking order was neither made public nor told to him.

The petition asked for the order and the related papers to be produced in court, for it to be stayed, and for the page to be restored until the hearing. It also raised the question of where transparency and due process are protected in such actions to block content. At the first hearing on 26 October the court asked both the Centre and the Kerala government whether either had asked for the page to be blocked, and sent a notice to Meta as well.

The government counsel replied that Meta had only been asked to remove a few comments under a few posts, and that there was no direction to shut the whole page. On the strength of that statement Justice Ziyad Rahman A.A. ordered on 5 November that the page could be run again after removing the comments named by the state police chief or officers under him, and that Meta would take the necessary steps.
According to SFLC.in, the organisation helping Nokaip, the block badly hit both the platform's reach and its earnings, though the report gives no figures for the loss.
nazar: This case shows how blurred censorship has become. The government says it did not ask for the page to be blocked, the company says it blocked it on the government's notice, and in between a small news platform stays cut off from its readers for five weeks. When orders stay hidden and no one is responsible, the loss always falls on the one who asks questions.
sawal: Who will pay for an order that no one actually gave?
ref: Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act

This section obliges platforms to remove unlawful content once they get a government notice.
If they do not, they can lose the protection from legal liability for users' content.

h: Three thousand kilometres in nine days: the elephants' journey from Assam to temples
dek: The Supreme Court expressed concern over the haste in sending elephants from Assam to Tamil Nadu, but said they cannot now be put through the ordeal of being sent back.
body: On 5 November the bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi expressed deep concern in the matter of captive elephants sent from Assam to Tamil Nadu. In a petition by People for Cattle in India the allegation is that the legal process fixed for sending these elephants was bypassed. This report is by The Wire, and The News Minute carried it.

Senior advocate Meenakshi Arora, appearing for the petitioner, said such a transfer involves several rounds of checks, approvals and consultation, which usually take at least fifty days. Here the application was made on 4 September and by 13 September the elephant had reached Chennai, a journey of roughly three thousand kilometres in nine days. She also placed before the court a table of the date of every clearance.

The Centre has a five-year-old elephant, Durga, who was handed over to the Meenakshi Amman temple in Madurai. According to the report, a religious body called Seva Trust gave her as a 'gift', and gave four more young elephants to temples in Nagapattinam, Kanchipuram and Tiruvannamalai. The trust is run by the wife of a man described in an earlier News Minute investigation as close to senior central leaders.

The bench accepted that all the elephants had been sent and that they cannot be put through the hardship of being returned. The Chief Justice said that had the court known earlier it would have intervened. The bench also repeated that no High Court or state government can go against its directions in force since 2021, which cover the identification of captive elephants, the checking of ownership and an audit of their transport.
nazar: An elephant is not a gift box to be sent from one corner of the country to another in nine days on the strength of influence. The court's helplessness stings too: the rules were broken, but the result cannot be reversed, because putting the animal through the same ordeal again would be the greater cruelty. When haste itself becomes the rescue, the law will always stay a step behind.
sawal: On whose word did a clearance meant to take fifty days come in nine?
ref: Transfer of captive elephants

Under the wildlife protection law, taking a captive elephant from one state to another needs the written approval of the Chief Wildlife Warden.
The Supreme Court has been monitoring this since 2021.

h: The Virudhunagar blast: the holiday wage that cost lives
dek: In a blast at a firecracker factory in Tamil Nadu on a Sunday, 25 workers were killed, 21 of them women. PARI's photographer spoke to the families left behind.
body: 19 April 2026 was a Sunday. The rules say firecracker units stay shut on holidays, yet work was on at the Vanaja Fireworks factory near Kattanarpatti village in Virudhunagar district. The gunpowder work that should be over by nine in the morning went on until three in the afternoon of that sweltering day. Twenty-five people died in the blast. PARI's photographer M. Palani Kumar went to the homes that no one came back to.

Twenty-one of the dead were women. Most had come for the extra Sunday wage and a cash bonus, because the two days after were election holidays and someone had a debt to clear, someone had fees to pay, someone had medicine to buy. Nineteen of the 25 were from the Muttaraiyar community and six were Dalit. Nineteen people from a single village had gone.

What the families say makes one picture: a sick or disabled husband, children at school and a mother running the home who had been at this work for twenty-five or thirty years. Fourteen-year-old Jaimurugan lost both parents. Farming here depends on rain and water is scarce, so even graduates work in firecrackers.

Workers say why accidents happen: more chemicals mixed than needed, gunpowder store and mixing in one place, twenty or thirty people in a room built for four. Word of an inspection always arrives first. According to the report, the factory's licence was suspended, yet work went on.

The government gave 5.5 lakh rupees to each family and the Fireworks Manufacturers Association gave three lakh. Bheemrao of the Dalit Liberation Movement recalls that after a 2021 blast the National Green Tribunal ordered 20 lakh rupees for each dead worker's family, and the same amount should be paid now. By his count, in about 11 years roughly 384 workers have been killed in some 22 blasts, the largest share of them Dalit, while the industry is worth more than six thousand crore rupees a year.
nazar: The light that scatters in the sky every Diwali is paid for with their lives by the women of Virudhunagar, and that price is added to no bill. The rules exist, but this report makes clear that the machinery enforcing them either arrives late or gives warning first.

The families' demands are very modest: some support in the summer months, work finished early in the morning, strict supervision. In an industry where most of the dead are women of Dalit and backward castes, ignoring safety is not mere carelessness, it is a social decision too.
sawal: In the light of firecrackers, whose life is burning?
ref: National Green Tribunal (NGT)
A special tribunal set up for matters related to the environment. In the 2021 Achangulam blast it took cognisance on its own and ordered 20 lakh rupees for the families of the dead.
Sivakasi-Virudhunagar
The region of Tamil Nadu where most of the country's firecrackers are made. Because farming here is dry, a large part of the villages depends on this work.

h: A loan of one lakh, a recovery of fifty lakh, and a kidney
dek: Roshan Kule, a farmer from Minthur village in Chandrapur, borrowed money to treat sick cows. The first part of PARI's three-part series shows how that loan became a trap.
body: March 2021, the second wave of Covid. Lumpy skin disease struck the twelve Jersey cows of Roshan Kule, a small farmer from Minthur village in Chandrapur district. Six cows died and an income of about 80,000 rupees a month from milk stopped. A bank loan was hard to get, so he borrowed one lakh rupees from a private moneylender in Brahmapuri.

Roshan alleges that the moneylender set the terms of returning the money within fifteen days, twenty per cent interest and a fine of 5,000 rupees every day, and that he was beaten when he objected. Then he was passed from one moneylender to another, and he says he was forced to borrow from cooperative societies, microfinance companies and banks as well.

Based on diaries and bank accounts, investigators have accepted that Roshan paid about fifty lakh rupees, while he himself says 72-75 lakh. The house is mortgaged to four institutions, the gold is gone, the tractor was seized and the four acres his father bought were sold cheap. Many nights the family slept hungry.

In 2024, looking for a way out of the pressure, Roshan reached a kidney-selling gang through Facebook and went to Cambodia and sold his kidney. In 2025 he was sent to scam compounds in Laos, from where he was freed. In November 2025 his wife Rohini tried to take her own life. The next day the family's story ran on a local TV channel, and only then was an FIR filed.

The police have filed a first chargesheet of about six thousand pages. The investigation found that not one of the six moneylenders was registered. Arrested in December 2025, these moneylenders are now on bail. The family now runs on Rohini's 7,500-rupee anganwadi salary, the father's pension and the brother's daily wage, and a large part of the salary goes into instalments.
nazar: Several committees on farmer suicides in Vidarbha have shown that the moneylending system running alongside the banks is a big cause, yet in official data this debt barely shows up. Roshan's story shows that when formal credit does not come at the hour of need, even one sick cow can sink a whole family.
This is not one farmer's bad luck; it is the failure of a system in which illegal moneylenders run without fear for years and the police move only when a camera reaches the spot.
sawal: Why does a farmer find the moneylender before the bank?
ref: Lumpy skin disease
A viral disease of cattle in which lumps appear on the body and milk yield falls. In 2020-22 it affected lakhs of animals in many states.
Minthur series
Jaideep Hardikar's three-part report for PARI. This first part is the story of the debt; the later parts go on to the sale of the kidney and the scam compounds in Laos.

h: Mango orchards cut, land gone on a 33-year lease, in return a 10x12 room
dek: In Pirpainti in Bhagalpur, 479 hectares of land were given to Adani Power on a 33-year lease. The 68 Adivasi families are getting one room each, and their names are in no document at all.
body: In Pirpainti in Bhagalpur district, a hundred metres from the road, is a Santal tola, about a dozen Santal Adivasi homes. Day and night, the sound of hundreds of trucks reversing, the rumble of bulldozers. Sunil Soren, 51, complains first that he cannot sleep. Then he says the real trouble is bigger: a 2,400 MW thermal power plant is coming up here, and he loses both his home and his farm labour. The land has been given to Adani Power, and work began in early 2026.

479 hectares were given to Adani Power Limited in August 2025 on a 33-year lease, two months before the Bihar election. Of this, 400 hectares is private land and 79 hectares government land. Santal and Sauria Paharia families have lived on this 'private' land for generations, but there are no papers in their names. The villagers did not even know, until money began reaching the landowners in December 2025. The Adani group's environmental impact assessment report does not mention Adivasis at all, so there is no resettlement or compensation plan either.

A public hearing was held in January 2026. Riju Paharia came to know of it from someone else; she went with dozens of people and gave the BDO a letter with her concerns, but her name is not in the attendance register of the hearing. Of the 68 families to be moved, 52 are Sauria Paharia and 16 Santal; the Sauria Paharia are a particularly vulnerable tribal group (PVTG). The government document made after the hearing carries the signatures of 447 people, among them one or two Sauria Paharia and not a single Santal. A day before the hearing, people speaking against it were held in custody under Section 126 (BNS) from nine in the morning to five in the evening; they were let go after the hearing was over.

In the name of resettlement, 71 rooms are being built on the company's land five kilometres away, each 10x12 feet, with a small kitchen. The Adivasis allege the rooms have no pillars and the roof is asbestos; one contractor said they were building to the size the company specified, but the reporter could not independently verify this. Sanjhli Marandi has three large rooms and six goats and chickens; she asks how all this will fit into one room. The BDO says ownership will come; the mutation has already been done.

Their livelihood has gone with it. In the mango orchards people had work all year, 400 to 700 rupees a day. According to the report, lakhs of mango and fruit trees have been uprooted in less than a year; one timber auction document mentions three lakh trees on 400 acres, while Shravan Singh's NGT petition speaks of five to ten lakh fruit trees, including five lakh mango trees 25-30 years old. People say groundwater has also gone down since the digging began.
nazar: Everything is in the papers except the Adivasis: no mention in the environmental impact assessment, no signatures in the hearing document, and on the day of the hearing they were held in custody. Consent was not built, it was only made on paper.

Adivasis are 1.5 per cent of Bihar's population, so they are electorally invisible and helpless before the administration and the company. Set 479 hectares and a 33-year lease against the offer of 71 rooms, and the bargaining becomes clear.
sawal: Why is a ten-by-twelve room enough in exchange for an orchard whose shade raised three generations?
ref: Sauria Paharia

An Adivasi community among Bihar's particularly vulnerable tribal groups (PVTGs); their population in the state is about 7,444. They are the largest number among the families to be displaced in Pirpainti.
Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)
A study done before a big project, which has to account for the effect on land, water, air and the people living there, and a public hearing is held.
photo_note: Representative image: a mango orchard in Bihar

h: Lions by the Tigris: one doorway left in Mosul's rubble
dek: Zardasht Ahmed's film on Al Jazeera Witness, set in post-ISIL Mosul, follows three men to ask whose heritage a ruined city is.
body: The Iraqi city of Mosul stands on the Tigris and its history is believed to be some eight thousand years old. From 2014 to 2017 the city was under ISIL control, and in the battle to free it a large part of the old city turned to rubble. Zardasht Ahmed's film, shown on Al Jazeera's programme Witness, begins its story with a marble doorway standing in that rubble, with two lions carved above it.

The doorway is the only part left of Bashar's family home. Bashar is a fisherman by trade, and his large ancestral house collapsed in the battle to free Mosul. He now guards the door, as if everything lost with the house survives in this stone.

The second character is Fakhri, a former soldier who collects old things in his passion for saving the city's heritage. He has an informal museum of his own and wants the doorway with the lions to come there. A big part of the film rests on the long conversation and bargaining between Bashar and Fakhri over this doorway.

The third character is Fazil, Fakhri's friend and a violinist. Music was banned under ISIL rule and artists like Fazil were robbed of their voice. Now he wants to bring melody back to the city. According to the film's synopsis, it is he who reminds Fakhri that behind every old object hides someone's loss.

In this way the film takes the question of heritage out of a bookish debate and into everyday life: is a broken house a family's memory or the whole city's inheritance? Is putting it in a museum saving it, or taking away someone's last support? The lions carved on the doorway become, in the film, signs of both stubbornness and cultural survival.

Zardasht Ahmed wrote, directed and shot the film himself. It is a co-production of Norway and the Netherlands, with archival material from an Iraqi company. The film's world premiere was in 2025 in the human rights competition at Copenhagen's CPH:DOX festival, and it received a special mention at Armenia's Golden Apricot film festival.
nazar: News from cities after war usually shrinks to a count of buildings and a reconstruction budget. This film reminds us that heritage is not only stone, it is also the memory of the people whose homes were destroyed. A culture that takes away an ordinary person's last support in the name of saving it is also a kind of eviction.

Here too, from Ayodhya to Banaras, old neighbourhoods have been torn down in the name of heritage and beautification. Mosul's Bashar forces us to ask for whom heritage is saved, and who pays its price.
sawal: In saving heritage, whose home is put at stake?
ref: Mosul
A large city in northern Iraq, on the Tigris. It was under ISIL control from 2014 to 2017 and the old city was badly destroyed in the battle to free it.
Witness
Al Jazeera English's documentary programme, which shows films by independent filmmakers from around the world on the lives of ordinary people.

h: Stones falling from a rooftop, and a girl's 'cholera' death
dek: In the tenth part of the 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' (the land of dead souls) series, Neha Naruka tells the story of a small town's rooftop, an outspoken girl, and her quietly buried death.
body: Neha Naruka's series of death stories on Sammukh, 'Mritatmaon ka Desh' (the land of dead souls), has reached its tenth part. At the start the writer asks herself what is new in such stories, when newspapers are full of such news every day. She thinks lightly about routes like research writing, a job in advertising or giving up writing, and in the end chooses to keep writing.

At the centre of the story is a girl from the neighbourhood whom the writer calls Chammakchhallo. She used to throw stones from the rooftop into the neighbours' courtyards, and when caught she would take her brother's name. The family would lock the door to the roof, but she would get up there on the excuse of drying clothes or checking the tank. One stone fell near the writer too, and the old women sitting in the courtyard pronounced their verdict on the girl's 'ways'.

Then the story drops suddenly into darkness. According to the writer, the girl's mother had told her to stay indoors, she did not listen, and her father took her life. In the neighbourhood this was put down as a death from cholera. Some time later the father died too, and people tied it to the curse of killing a daughter.

The writer opens another thread: in the house where the most stones fell there was a boy who studied on the rooftop, who disappeared the same day and came back later with a government job and dowry matches. She calls this gossip and also imagines that the stones may have been thrown aiming at him. The real thing, she says, only the father knew.

Against this she sets another episode from the neighbourhood, where a boy who did obscene things from a rooftop in front of women was let off as 'just a boy'. People advised the gun-owning father to go into politics. This irony hangs over the whole piece.
nazar: Naruka's prose moves in the language of banter and then suddenly comes to rest on a death that the whole neighbourhood forgot by calling it an illness. This almost careless tone is what leaves the reader more unsettled.

In our view this piece says more about 'honour killing' than any report: a woman's desire is a crime, a man's indecency is 'the way of boys', and the one who commits violence is seen as having a future in politics.
sawal: Which death does a neighbourhood forget by calling it an illness?
ref: Mritatmaon ka Desh
Neha Naruka's series of death stories on Sammukh, in which the anonymous deaths of small-town life are recorded in a mix of memoir and fiction.
Neha Naruka

A Hindi poet, author of the collection 'Fati Hatheliyan'.
According to her writer's note on Sammukh, she received the 2024 Vagishwari Samman.

h: In a marriage, where self-respect ends and ego begins
dek: In the fifth part of the 'Daampatya' column, Pallavi Vinod uses the stories of three homes to show how patriarchy feeds the ego and hollows out a relationship.
body: Pallavi Vinod's column 'Daampatya' on Sammukh looks at marriage apart from the romantic glow of rituals. In the fifth part her opening point is plain: a good partner is one who shares the daily burden, laughs with you at small things and stands by you in difficulty.

The axis of the essay is the difference between self-respect and ego. According to the writer, self-respect protects oneself without hurting the partner, while ego is a hard shell that wounds everyone who comes close. Ego rises from frustration inside, self-respect from good intent, and it includes respect for others.

She ties this directly to patriarchy, which builds a ladder of ruler and ruled within one family and puts money and power above every other contribution, when a home runs on love, care, time and earnings together. Leaning on Kabir's famous line that 'I' and love cannot live together, she says this is easy to understand and hard to live by.

Three stories give the argument body. In one, a wife from a rich home keeps mocking her husband's ordinary family, and years later the daughter is cut off from her grandparents. In another, a mother-in-law praised during Covid for her social work discriminates against her sick daughter-in-law. In the third, the husband slaps his wife, who was right in a petty quarrel at a cinema; years later she recognises his behaviour as the signs of a narcissistic personality disorder.

The writer also accepts that women too taunt and humiliate, over a husband's earnings or his family duties. At the end she asks the reader to look within: if your partner is suffocating under your behaviour, you have failed as a human being.
nazar: This essay can also be read as advice, but its strength is in its stories, which break the habit of waving away domestic violence and humiliation as 'a husband-wife matter'.
In our view the most important thing is that the writer sees ego not as a personal flaw but as the product of a structure of power. Equality inside the home is a question of democracy too.
sawal: What conversation can begin equality inside a home?
ref: Narcissistic personality disorder
A mental condition in which a person sees himself as exceptional, is hungry for praise and cares little for others' feelings.
Kabir
A 15th-century saint-poet whose verses are known for their bite against ego, hypocrisy and caste.

h: 'Gondhal': where the folk ritual becomes a character in the story
dek: Vani Tripathi Tikku's review of the Marathi film that is India's official entry for the Oscars, which warns against haste in celebration even as it praises.
body: On Janaki Pul, the actor, theatre person and writer Vani Tripathi Tikku has written at length on Santosh Dawkhar's Marathi film 'Gondhal'. According to the writer, the Film Federation of India chose it out of 33 films as India's official entry for the international feature film category at the 99th Academy Awards. She makes clear this is a selection, not a nomination.

Gondhal is a folk-religious performance from Maharashtra, tied to the worship of Bhavani and Khandoba. On marriages and auspicious occasions, Gondhali performers sing, dance, act and tell stories all night to seek the goddess's blessing. According to the review, this tradition has also been a way of passing myths, local history and social values from generation to generation.

The film's story is of Suman (Ishita Deshmukh), trapped in a stifling marriage to the wealthy Anand, while her heart is tied to the Gondhali performer Sahiba. Anand's cousin Sarjerav is besotted with Suman, and Suman turns his infatuation into a plot that goes as far as a plan for murder. On the night of the Gondhal, the lines between performance and reality, devotion and deceit begin to blur. Above them all hangs the shadow of the feudal headman Abasaheb Patil.

What draws the writer most is that Suman is neither a helpless victim nor a simple villain; she takes deliberate decisions and wants control of her life back through relationships. The ritual here is not background but part of the plot. The film also asks how a society that celebrates devotion tolerates injustice.

The review also reins in the celebration. The writer recalls that after 'Shwaas', 'Harishchandrachi Factory' and 'Court', this is the fourth Marathi entry, and India has never won. Instead of selling folk culture to foreign audiences as a 'wonder', the film should first be judged as cinema, and the country should put its many voices forward with confidence.
nazar: This review is valuable because it looks at the film outside the frame of Hindi, star-led 'representative cinema', and treats folk tradition not as decoration but as a stage for the debate over power and desire.
In our view its warning about the habit of turning the Oscar race into a 'national victory' is just as necessary.
sawal: Do films made on folk traditions reach their own audiences?
ref: Gondhal
A folk-religious performance of Maharashtra, in which Gondhali performers sing, dance and tell stories all night in praise of Bhavani and Khandoba.
Waghya-Murali
The men (waghya) and women (murali) who are servant-performers in the Khandoba tradition, and have long taken part in folk songs and all-night vigils.
photo_note: A gathering of musicians, Raja Ravi Varma

h: The 'anti-library' president who broke a hundred-year tradition
dek: Alex H. Poole, a professor of information science, has combed the statements of seventeen American presidents to show how Donald Trump stands apart on libraries.
body: In Dawn's 'Books and Authors', an essay by Alex H. Poole, associate professor at Drexel University, opens with a statement from 31 March 2026, when Trump said his presidential library would probably be a hotel with Air Force One kept in its lobby, and that he does not believe in building libraries or museums.

Poole has read the speeches and official papers of seventeen presidents from 1923 to now, and material from the American Library Association. According to him, presidents of both parties have called libraries the foundation of democracy and informed citizenship. Roosevelt warned against leaders who want to decide what the public reads; Eisenhower, speaking against censorship during the 'Red Scare', signed a law for rural libraries; Kennedy said libraries should be open to all except the censor.

The chain runs on to Reagan, Clinton, Obama and Biden. Obama called libraries a way of telling truth from falsehood and opposed bans on books; Biden in a 2022 executive order called library services essential.

Trump breaks from this tradition. The writer counts that in 2019 he mocked Narendra Modi's claim of building a library in Afghanistan; at the start of the second term a post in the education department that kept watch on book bans was abolished; in March 2025 came an order to abolish the federal body that funds libraries and museums, which a court stopped.

In May 2025 the head of the Library of Congress, Carla Hayden, was removed, the first woman and the first African-American to hold the post; the reasons cited included 'DEI' and 'inappropriate books' for children. The essay ends with a speech in September 2026 in which Trump accused opposition candidates of wanting to fill children's libraries with books by Lenin and Stalin.
nazar: This essay builds no grand theory; it only sets the documents in order, and that order becomes the biggest argument: an attack on the library is really an attack on the people's right to know.
In our view it holds a mirror for Indian readers too, where chapters are dropped from syllabuses and books are stopped in the name of 'hurt sentiments'.
sawal: When did you last look at the state of your city's public library?
ref: Institute of Museum and Library Services
A US federal agency, the largest government body that gives grants to libraries and museums across the country.
Red Scare
The anti-communist frenzy in 1950s America, in which writers, teachers and books were targeted on suspicion of 'treason'.
photo_note: An illustrated manuscript of the Kalpasutra

h: From Almora to Heidelberg: the unseen threads of the freedom struggle
dek: Divya Aslesha's review of Devki Pande's first novel 'The Imitation Englishman', which sees the Ghadar and Hindu-German conspiracy years through a young man's eyes.
body: On Scroll, Divya Aslesha reviews Devki Pande's first novel 'The Imitation Englishman' (Bloomsbury India). The story begins in 1916, when Madhusudan, twenty years old, from Almora, goes to Heidelberg in Germany to study law, while his elder brother becomes a soldier and is sent to north Africa in the First World War.

On the sea voyage he meets Ameer Farooqi of Rawalpindi, who is part of the Hindu-German conspiracy that gathered arms for rebellion against British rule. A beating of soldiers at a bar in Germany sharpens Madhusudan's political understanding. Ameer goes to America, joins the Ghadar movement and is killed during the San Francisco trial; Madhusudan reaches London, where he faces racism at an imaginary university, forms an Indian Association, and finally returns as a lawyer, having lost his brother and his dreams to the empire.

According to the reviewer, the novel's strength is that it does not see the freedom struggle in one colour. It has armed revolutionaries, big leaders, people who stood with the British, and those who hollowed out the Raj from within. Its eye on race and class in London is sharp, especially on those rich Hindustani friends busy becoming 'imitation Englishmen'.

But the flaws are not few either. The two parts feel like two different stories, at the start Ameer's character outweighs the protagonist, the conspiracy thread is dropped as soon as London is reached, the early prose and dialogue are contrived, and the balance between history and story wobbles. The reviewer also notes that despite a high-caste hero the novel avoids the question of caste.
Even so, she found the book fast-paced and relevant, especially in October, when protests across the country were borrowing the language of the freedom struggle.
nazar: This review weighs the novel's praise and criticism honestly. The most interesting thing is that it puts a finger on the absence of caste, which is the old silence of most stories of the freedom struggle.

In our view bringing the forgotten stories of Ghadar and migrant revolutionaries back into fiction is necessary work in itself, especially when the effort to fit the history of independence into a single frame is gathering pace.
sawal: Why does caste show up so little in stories of the freedom struggle?
ref: Ghadar movement
A revolutionary movement of migrant Hindustanis, mostly Punjabis, in America and Canada from 1913, which tried to overthrow British rule by armed rebellion.
Hindu-German conspiracy
A joint plan of Indian revolutionaries and Germany during the First World War, on which a long trial ran in San Francisco in 1917-18.

h: 'Joothi Gali': the country's dark present, packed into one lane
dek: Poet Pawan Karan's review of Rishikesh Sulabh's new novel, in which religion is a tool of property and dominance, and every lane is slowly turning 'joothi'.
body: On The Wire Hindi, the poet Pawan Karan has reviewed Rishikesh Sulabh's novel 'Joothi Gali' (the defiled lane), which he sees as a sequel to Sulabh's earlier novel 'Data Peer'. The story is of one lane, where every family has some scheme: to grow its wealth, to protect its property or to grab another's. Right in the middle of all these plans sits religion.

According to the reviewer, religious hatred has turned every lane in the country into a 'joothi gali', and rich colonies and high-rise flats are no different: the same forced donations, the heavy pandal, the DJ, and someone who has decided he is the contractor of religion.

At the centre of the story is Bambam Bhaiya, the head of the 'Veer Hanuman Dal', the biggest product of this atmosphere. On the excuse of a crack in the Hanuman idol he takes over the temple, the priest and the nearby shop are evicted, and later a friend of his opens a shop for worship goods there. Some students of the lane are picked up by men posing as police or as terrorists, taking them for Muslims; who they were and what happened to the students, the novel leaves to the reader.

Pawan Karan praises Sulabh's fine, realistic portraiture, and the way he handles a serious subject with light irony and does not pour ghee on communal fire. Jankadulari, who gives Bambam Bhaiya a sharp answer, and Babbo, who forms her own gang of girls, seem to him memorable.

The criticism is clear too. According to the reviewer, many women are defined only by the men around them and by old moulds, the characters are so dense that before one picture clears the next arrives, and no organised resistance to the misuse of power appears in the novel. Still, the near-inevitable path of justice devised for the lane's injustice seems to him proof of the writer's craft.
nazar: This review uses the novel to put a finger on the changed face of our neighbourhoods: religion is now less faith and more a business of capture and earning, and its contractor is the lane's new boss.

In our view the reviewer's question about the absence of resistance is the most important. If literature only draws a map of the dark and does not see those who fight it, it tells only half the truth.
sawal: Who made themselves the contractor of religion in your lane?
ref: Rishikesh Sulabh
A Hindi fiction writer and playwright; according to the review, 'Joothi Gali' comes after his novel 'Data Peer'.
Data Peer
Rishikesh Sulabh's earlier novel, which the reviewer sees as the backdrop to 'Joothi Gali'.
photo_note: A lane in Rania village, about 1816
